title: Neutron
summary: A neutron is a particle in the nucleus with no electric charge at all. It adds mass to the atom and is the particle whose count changes between isotopes of the same element.

processes: Varying between isotopes of an element
plainLanguageExplanation: A neutron is the quiet particle of the atom. It lives in the nucleus right beside the proton, and it weighs about the same as a proton — but it carries no electric charge at all. Neutrons are neutral, hence the name. So what does a neutron do? First, it adds mass: because neutrons sit in the nucleus, they make the atom heavier without changing its charge. An atom with extra neutrons is heavier than one without, even though it is the same element. Second — and this is the famous job — the neutron count is the only count that can change without changing the element. Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes. Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons; carbon-14 has 8. Same element, same protons, but different neutrons and different masses. Neutrons also help glue the nucleus together: the positive protons push each other apart, and the charge-free neutrons add a kind of extra grip that keeps the nucleus stable. Quiet, uncharged, but essential.

keyFacts.label: Charge
keyFacts.value: None — the neutron is electrically neutral

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: In the nucleus, beside the protons

keyFacts.label: Weight
keyFacts.value: About the same mass as a proton

keyFacts.label: The key job
keyFacts.value: Its count varies between isotopes without changing the element

keyFacts.label: Stability
keyFacts.value: Helps hold the nucleus together against proton repulsion

keyFacts.label: Example
keyFacts.value: Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons; carbon-14 has 8 — both are carbon

whyItMatters: Neutrons explain isotopes, atomic mass, and nuclear stability. They are why the same element can come in different weights — carbon-12 and carbon-14 — and why archaeologists use those differences to date ancient objects. The neutron is the silent partner that makes nuclear physics and isotope chemistry possible.
tagline: The silent weight of the nucleus
didYouKnow: Carbon-14, the isotope used to date ancient bones, has two extra neutrons compared to ordinary carbon — and those extra neutrons are what make it slowly tick away like a clock.
compareReason: The neutron and proton are inseparable neighbors in the nucleus — comparing them makes the neutron's lack of charge, and the proton's defining charge, both unforgettable.
